clue.text: Nursery rhyme from storytelling show cut by a third: presenter unwell

indicators.note: the show's nine-letter title loses its final third, three letters off the end

parts.note: Jackanory was a long-running BBC children's television programme in which a guest read stories aloud
a DJ, or disc jockey, presents a music programme
someone unwell is ill

explanation.surface: A critic reviews a children's TV programme trimmed back, while its host is off sick.
explanation.walkthrough: JACKANORY is a British children's TV show in which stories were read; 'cut by a third' removes ORY, leaving JACKAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The pair who went up the hill to fetch a pail of water star in a famous English nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Drink half of just frozen water

indicators.note: only the opening half of the four-letter word just is kept

parts.note: water that has frozen is ice

explanation.surface: A drinker orders something simple: just water, frozen.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit juice is a common soft drink, so the noun names a type of beverage.

clue.text: Changing a reformed group of prisoners

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are formed again into a new order

explanation.surface: Reforming convicts: a group of prisoners being changed for the better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' reads as prison rehabilitation, but it signals rearranging CHANGING A.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain gang is a team of convicts chained together for outdoor labour.

clue.text: Chopper with a cross on rotating handle

parts.note: a cross is the letter X

indicators.note: the word for a handle turns round so it reads backwards

parts.note: a handle is slang for a name

explanation.surface: An axe described: a chopper with a cross-shaped piece on a turning handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handle' is slang for a name; 'rotating' turns NAME into EMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who wields an axe chops, so a chopper is a fair cryptic description of an axe-wielder.

clue.text: Useless Edmund ignoring odd characters

indicators.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the name are dropped, keeping the even-placed ones

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses Edmund as useless for ignoring odd people.
explanation.definitionFit: A dud is something that fails to work, so as an adjective it means worthless or ineffective.

clue.text: One, then two marks added to spoken exam — that's unethical!

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
M is an abbreviation for mark (the old German currency), so two of them give MM
an oral is an examination taken by speaking

explanation.surface: A student is outraged that extra marks were added to someone's oral exam result.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe conduct that breaks moral principles; they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Method of calculating the Great Wall of China, say?

definitions.meaning: a written arithmetic procedure for dividing large numbers step by step

definitions.text: the Great Wall of China, say?
definitions.meaning: the wall is a very lengthy barrier separating one region from another

explanation.surface: A puzzled pupil wonders how one would calculate the size of the Great Wall of China.
explanation.definitionFit: The arithmetic method is a standard school technique; the wall is a huge partition stretching thousands of miles.

clue.text: Chicken with batter — or a different bird

parts.note: chicken in the sense of cowardly, which is yellow
a hammer is something that batters or pounds

explanation.surface: A menu offers chicken in batter, or perhaps some other fowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' and 'batter' suggest food, but they are cowardly and a pounding tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowhammer is a small yellow-headed bunting, a European songbird, so a bird other than a chicken.

clue.text: Leave the country, missing golf in Dubai?

indicators.note: the letter for golf is absent from the word

parts.note: to leave one's country to live abroad is to emigrate
Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone considers leaving the country but would miss their golf in Dubai.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is one of the seven states of the United Arab Emirates, an example, flagged by the question mark.

clue.text: Devil's lair imprisoning little Maureen

indicators.note: the den holds the short name captive within it

parts.note: an animal's lair is its den
Mo is a short form of the name Maureen

explanation.surface: A devil's lair holds a girl called Maureen captive, like a fairytale villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A demon is an evil spirit, synonymous with a devil.

clue.text: We initial forms to prepare for attack

indicators.note: the letters of the two words form a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Officers initial forms before a military attack, a piece of bureaucratic preparation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forms' looks like paperwork, but it is the verb signalling a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is to stay hidden ready to ambush someone, a preparation for an assault.

clue.text: Re-attempt shifting diminutive bouncer

indicators.note: the letters shift about into a new order

explanation.surface: A small nightclub bouncer tries again to move someone along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouncer' suggests a doorman, but it is something you bounce on.
explanation.definitionFit: A trampette is a small trampoline used in gymnastics, so a little thing to bounce on.

clue.text: Free travel by horse without tail

indicators.note: the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to travel on horseback is to ride

explanation.surface: An offer of free horse travel, though the horse has no tail.
explanation.definitionFit: To rid someone of something is to free them of it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Battles a western city

parts.note: battles are wars

explanation.surface: Battles rage over a city in the west.
explanation.definitionFit: Warsaw is the capital of Poland, an example of a city.

clue.text: Worked miracle to recover

indicators.note: the letters are worked over into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A worked miracle allowed someone to recover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked miracle' reads as a healing, but 'Worked' signals rearranging MIRACLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reclaim something is to get it back, a synonym for retrieving it.

clue.text: Russian scientist who regularly produced a dog's dinner?

definitions.meaning: a physiologist famous for experiments on conditioned reflexes

definitions.text: who regularly produced a dog's dinner?
definitions.meaning: in those experiments dogs were fed at regular signals, so the scientist routinely supplied canine meals

explanation.surface: A Russian researcher is mocked for routinely making a mess of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a dog's dinner' is British slang for a mess; here it is read literally, as food for his laboratory dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan Pavlov was the Russian physiologist who fed dogs after a bell to study conditioned reflexes.

clue.text: Badger has to eat tops of radishes and swedes

indicators.note: the word has takes the initials inside it, as if swallowing them
the first letter of each of the three words is taken

explanation.surface: A badger snuffles up the tops of radishes and swedes in a vegetable garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal 'Badger' is the verb definition. Swede is the British name for rutabaga.
explanation.definitionFit: To badger someone is to pester them persistently, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Curvature observed in turning aircraft

indicators.note: the run of letters is read backwards
the letters are seen within the word that follows

explanation.surface: Pilots notice the curve an aircraft traces as it banks.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc is a curved line or a segment of a circle, so it names a curve.

clue.text: Bar supporters from the football ground?

definitions.text: Bar supporters from the football ground?

parts.words: Bar supporters from the football ground?
parts.note: reads like rowdy pub-going fans, but the bar is the crossbar, held up by two uprights

explanation.surface: Fans from the stadium are banned from the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub or a ban; it is the crossbar of the goal.
explanation.definitionFit: The upright posts hold up the crossbar at each end of a football pitch.

clue.text: Time church benches must be lifted and brushed

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters reads them from bottom to top

parts.note: church benches are pews

explanation.surface: In time, church benches must be raised and swept underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' reverses the pieces in a down clue: T plus PEWS read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Swept is the past tense of sweep, meaning cleaned with a brush.

clue.text: Call for Tom to cut grass around one area

indicators.note: the mowing word goes around the two letters

parts.note: to cut grass is to mow
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone shouts for Tom to come and mow the lawn round an area.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom is not a person: a tom is a male cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, and its cry is the cat's characteristic mewing sound.

clue.text: Success with batting

parts.note: in cricket the side batting is in

explanation.surface: A batsman enjoys success at the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: A win is a victory, so it names a success.

clue.text: Style of fancy red coat

indicators.note: fancy as a verb or adjective suggests something elaborate, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fashion note describing the style of an elaborate red coat.
explanation.definitionFit: Art Deco is a decorative design style of the 1920s and 30s.

clue.text: Suggestive short skirts with modern clothing

indicators.note: the word for modern wraps round the skirts like a garment

parts.note: something modern is recent
minis are short skirts

explanation.surface: A fashion critic finds short skirts with modern clothing rather risqué.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggestive' hints at racy, but here it means evoking a memory.
explanation.definitionFit: Reminiscent means calling something to mind, so it is suggestive of it.
